paragraphs.context: Dawn was breaking in the Frog Creek woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack has a dream about the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: It is early morning. In a dream, Jack runs very fast through the woods toward a light. He is so fast that he cannot hear his feet or feel the cold air.

background.note: Frog Creek is the made-up town in Pennsylvania, USA, where Jack and Annie live.

paragraphs.context: As Jack got closer to the light
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the dream he sees Teddy and Kathleen.
paragraphs.simple: In his dream, Jack sees the tree house at the top of the tallest oak. A girl with dark wavy hair and a boy with messy red hair are waving at him from the window. Jack feels very happy.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. His sister, Annie, was standing beside his bed.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wakes Jack up very early.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wakes up. Annie is already wearing her winter jacket. It is still almost dark outside.

paragraphs.context: “I dreamed we were running through the woods at dawn,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she dreamed that they ran to the tree house and found Teddy and Kathleen waiting for them.

paragraphs.context: Annie left Jack's room. Jack jumped out of bed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack gets ready quickly and quietly.
paragraphs.simple: Jack quickly puts on his glasses and clothes, takes his jacket and backpack, and goes quietly downstairs and out of the house.

paragraphs.context: Annie was waiting on the porch. The February air was chilly.
paragraphs.simple: Annie waits outside. It is a cold February morning. The grass shines with frost as the sun comes up.

paragraphs.context: Jack nodded and zipped his jacket.
paragraphs.simple: Jack closes his jacket. Without talking, they hurry along their street and go into the woods. They run between the long morning shadows and the winter trees with no leaves.

paragraphs.context: The tree house was back, just as Jack had seen it in his dream!
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is really there.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is back in the tallest oak tree, exactly like in Jack's dream. It is shining in the cold morning light.

paragraphs.context: “I guess only part of this dream came true,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie climbs up and finds something.
paragraphs.simple: At first no one answers, so Annie thinks only part of the dream came true. She climbs up the rope ladder. Then she cries "Oh, wow!"

paragraphs.context: “They're here!” said Annie in a loud whisper.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy and Kathleen are sleeping in the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy and Kathleen, the young helpers of Morgan le Fay, are sitting under the window. They are wrapped in thick wool cloaks and are sleeping deeply.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is a magic librarian from the King Arthur stories. The tree house belongs to her.
Teddy is a young sorcerer and Kathleen is a "selkie" (a seal girl) from earlier Merlin Missions. Both are learning magic from Morgan.

paragraphs.context: Kathleen blinked and yawned. Teddy rubbed his eyes.
paragraphs.simple: Kathleen and Teddy wake up. Teddy smiles widely and jumps to his feet to say hello.

paragraphs.context: “Ah, then our magic worked!” said Teddy.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They sent the dream with magic.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy explains that Kathleen's idea was to send dreams to tell Jack and Annie they were here. The magic also made Teddy and Kathleen fall asleep.

paragraphs.context: “But now we are all awake,” said Kathleen.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kathleen is glad to see them.
paragraphs.simple: Kathleen stands up and pulls her cloak around her. Her blue eyes shine like the sea in the early light.

paragraphs.context: “Not exactly,” said Teddy. “Merlin has a most important mission for you.
paragraphs.mainIdea: This time Jack and Annie will go alone.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy says Merlin has a very important job for Jack and Annie, but Teddy and Kathleen will not go with them this time.

paragraphs.context: Teddy and Kathleen looked at each other and smiled.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan thinks they are ready to use magic.
paragraphs.simple: Kathleen says Morgan thinks Jack and Annie may be ready to use magic by themselves.

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” said Teddy, “but Merlin is very cautious
paragraphs.mainIdea: Merlin will test them on four missions.
paragraphs.simple: Merlin is careful about giving magic to ordinary people, even good ones like Jack and Annie, and about using magic outside Camelot. But Morgan has made him agree to let them show what they can do. They will have four missions as tests.

background.note: Camelot is the castle and city of King Arthur in the old stories. Merlin and Morgan live there.

paragraphs.context: “Remember what I told you on our last adventure?”
paragraphs.simple: Teddy reminds them of his words: if they all work together, anything is possible. Annie finishes the sentence, but she says that this time Teddy and Kathleen are not coming.

paragraphs.context: “That is true,” said Kathleen. “And that is why we bring you this.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kathleen gives them a small handmade book.
paragraphs.simple: Because they will not be there, Kathleen takes a small handmade book out of her cloak and gives it to Annie.

paragraphs.context: The cover of the book was made of rough brown paper.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book has a simple cover.
paragraphs.simple: The cover is made of rough brown paper. The title is written on it in neat, simple handwriting. (The title is shown as a picture in the book.)

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” said Kathleen. “One line of each rhyme is in Teddy's language
paragraphs.simple: Kathleen says each rhyme has one line in Teddy's language and one line in hers, the language of the Seal People.

background.note: In the earlier book "Summer of the Sea Serpent", Kathleen is one of the Seal People (selkies): in old Scottish and Irish stories, selkies are seals that can become people.

paragraphs.context: Annie opened the book to the table of contents.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They look at the list of rhymes.
paragraphs.simple: Annie opens the book at the list of rhymes. Jack and Annie read the list quickly, and Jack reads some names out loud.

paragraphs.context: Annie giggled. “These are so cool!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to try a rhyme now.
paragraphs.simple: Annie laughs and says the rhymes are great. She wants them all to turn into ducks right now.

paragraphs.context: “Not now,” said Kathleen. “You must use these rhymes very sparingly.
paragraphs.simple: Kathleen says they must use the rhymes very carefully. There are only ten, each one works only one time, and they must last for four trips.

paragraphs.context: “Aye,” said Teddy. “Merlin has agreed that if you can use our magic wisely
paragraphs.mainIdea: The prize for passing the tests.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy says that if they use the magic wisely on four missions, Merlin will teach them the secrets of making magic by themselves.

paragraphs.context: Jack put the book of magic rhymes in his backpack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy gives them the research book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts the rhyme book in his backpack and asks where they are going. Teddy gives him a book from Morgan with a picture of a bright city surrounded by water on the cover.

paragraphs.context: “I've heard of Venice,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie has heard of Venice before. Last year her aunt and uncle went there on vacation (a holiday trip).

background.note: Venice is a famous old city in the north of Italy. It is built on many small islands in the sea, and it has canals (waterways) instead of streets.

paragraphs.context: “Aye, 'tis a city that has long welcomed travelers,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: They will visit Venice of long ago.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy says yes, Venice has been happy to have visitors for a very long time. ("Aye, 'tis" is old English for "Yes, it is".) But Jack and Annie will go to the Venice of 260 years ago, in the 1700s.

paragraphs.context: “Merlin has prepared careful directions for you,”
paragraphs.simple: Merlin has written careful instructions for them. Teddy takes a letter out of his cloak, gives it to Jack and tells him to read it when they get to Venice.

paragraphs.context: “Wait a minute,” said Annie. “If we take the tree house to Venice
paragraphs.mainIdea: How will Teddy and Kathleen go home?
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks a question: if Jack and Annie take the tree house to Venice, how will Teddy and Kathleen get back to Camelot?

paragraphs.context: Teddy and Kathleen smiled and held up their hands.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Magic rings will take them home.
paragraphs.simple: Each of them wears a ring made of light blue glass. Kathleen says the rings are magic. They belong to Morgan, and they will take Teddy and Kathleen home.

paragraphs.context: “Remember,” Teddy said to Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy tells them to follow Merlin's instructions carefully. If they show that they are wise and brave helpers, Merlin will ask them to come again soon.

paragraphs.context: Kathleen and Teddy raised their glass rings to their lips.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy and Kathleen use the magic rings.
paragraphs.simple: They lift the glass rings up to their mouths. They whisper some words so quietly that no one can hear them, and then they blow on the rings.

paragraphs.context: Before Jack and Annie's eyes, the two young sorcerers began to fade
paragraphs.simple: While Jack and Annie watch, Teddy and Kathleen slowly become harder and harder to see in the cool morning air. Very quickly, they are completely gone.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath. Then he pointed at the cover of the Venice book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathes in deeply to feel calm. He points at the picture on the cover of the Venice book and wishes to go there. The wish makes the tree house start to travel.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. He and Annie were wearing purple and pink outfits
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their new clothes are very funny.
paragraphs.simple: They are wearing purple and pink clothes with big folded collars, funny hats and red slippers with big bows.

paragraphs.context: “I don't know,” said Jack. He didn't feel like a wise and brave helper
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not know who they are dressed as. In his red slippers, he does not feel wise and brave. He feels silly.

paragraphs.context: Together Jack and Annie looked out the tree house window.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They land in a walled garden.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is in a small tree in a garden with walls around it. The sky is gray. Jack cannot tell if it is morning or evening. The air is wet and heavy, as if a storm will start soon.

paragraphs.context: Today the city of Venice (say VEN-iss)
paragraphs.simple: Venice is very popular with tourists. It is in a lagoon of the Adriatic Sea. It has canals instead of roads. People travel in long, flat boats called gondolas. A gondolier stands at the back and pushes the boat with a long oar.

background.note: Gondolas are long, thin black boats. They have been used in Venice for about a thousand years and are now mostly used by tourists.

paragraphs.context: “Wait,” said Jack. “We don't even know what our mission is yet.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they do not know their job yet. He takes out Merlin's letter, opens it and reads it out. (The letter is shown as a picture in the book.)

paragraphs.context: “I wonder who the Grand Lady is,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie has questions about the letter.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wonders who the Grand Lady is and why they must save her.

paragraphs.context: “I'm wondering lots of stuff,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack has lots of questions. Why does the letter talk about the King of the Jungle when they are in a city? And who is the angel?

paragraphs.context: “Let's just take one thing at a time,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to do one thing at a time.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they should not think about everything at once. They should just do the first thing.

paragraphs.context: When waters rise beneath the moon,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The first line of the rhyme.
paragraphs.simple: When the water goes up under the moon (at night, at high tide),

paragraphs.context: Visit the Grand Lady of the Lagoon.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The second line of the rhyme.
paragraphs.simple: go and see the Grand Lady of the Lagoon.

paragraphs.context: Jack put Merlin's letter into his backpack
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts the letter, the research book and the rhyme book in his backpack and follows Annie down the ladder.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie walked over a pebbly path as the sky darkened.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is glad it is getting dark.
paragraphs.simple: They walk on a path of small stones as it gets dark. Jack is happy it is night, because he does not want anyone to see his silly clothes and red slippers.

paragraphs.context: “That must be the way out,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie finds a wooden gate in the garden wall and opens it.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie stepped through the gate onto a quiet, empty walkway.
paragraphs.simple: Outside the gate is a quiet path. Next to it is a narrow strip of water.

paragraphs.context: “And that must be a gondola,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie points at a long, curved black boat coming around the corner. It moves quietly up the canal toward them.

paragraphs.context: There were two people in the boat—a gondolier and a passenger.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The two people wear strange masks.
paragraphs.simple: In the boat are a gondolier and a passenger. Both wear black cloaks, white gloves and pale white masks with long noses like bird beaks. The passenger holds a lantern. The gondolier stands at the back with a long oar.

background.note: This kind of mask is like the old "plague doctor" mask of Venice, with a long beak. Today it is a popular Carnival mask.

paragraphs.context: The person's voice was muffled behind the white mask.
paragraphs.simple: The passenger's voice is not clear because of the mask. The passenger asks if they need help.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, of course. She is back that way!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The passenger knows the Grand Lady.
paragraphs.simple: The masked passenger says the Grand Lady is back that way and tells them to come.

paragraphs.context: “Great!” said Annie. She grabbed Jack's hand
paragraphs.simple: Annie pulls Jack to the gondola. The boat moves a little from side to side as they climb in and sit between the gondolier and the passenger.

paragraphs.context: The gondolier pushed the gondola away from the landing.
paragraphs.simple: The gondolier pushes the boat away from the place where boats stop. His oar makes soft splashes as they move up the canal.

paragraphs.context: Jack cleared his throat.
paragraphs.simple: Jack coughs a little and politely asks why they are wearing bird masks.

paragraphs.context: “For Carnival, of course,” said the passenger.
paragraphs.simple: The passenger says the masks are for Carnival, and thinks Jack and Annie are wearing clown costumes for Carnival too.

paragraphs.context: As the gondola slid through the canal
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack secretly takes out the book.
paragraphs.simple: As the boat moves smoothly along, Jack quietly takes the research book out of his backpack.

paragraphs.context: “I don't think they had roller coasters two hundred sixty years ago,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack whispers that there were no roller coasters 260 years ago.

paragraphs.context: For many centuries, Carnival has been the most famous yearly festival of Venice.
paragraphs.simple: Carnival has been the most famous festival in Venice for hundreds of years. People dress up as anything they like. During Carnival, rich and poor, men and women, young and old are all the same.

background.note: Carnival in Venice happens every year in the weeks before Lent (a time of fasting in the Christian year), usually in February. People wear masks and costumes.

paragraphs.context: “Look, that's us,” whispered Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their costumes are in the book.
paragraphs.simple: Annie finds a picture of a costume just like theirs: a white folded collar and red slippers with bows.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, and that's them,” whispered Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bird masks are in the book too.
paragraphs.simple: Jack points to a picture of a person in a black cloak and a white bird mask, like the people in the gondola.

paragraphs.context: Jack closed the book and put it away.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack still wonders about the danger.
paragraphs.simple: Now the gondola people do not seem so strange. But Jack still wonders why a grand lady is in great danger during Carnival.

paragraphs.context: As the boat glided around a bend, Jack caught his breath.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A wide canal full of boats.
paragraphs.simple: Around a corner, Jack sees many gondolas moving on the rough water of a wide canal. They have ribbons and flowers. The light from their lanterns dances on the dark water.

background.note: This is probably the Grand Canal, the biggest canal in Venice. It goes through the middle of the city in an "S" shape.

paragraphs.context: In the distance, thousands of candles twinkled along the shoreline.
paragraphs.simple: Far away, thousands of candles shine along the edge of the water. They hear people laughing, clapping and shouting.

paragraphs.context: “Hold on tightly!” said the masked person
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wind and waves get stronger.
paragraphs.simple: The masked person tells them to hold on because the tide is high. As their boat joins many others going to Carnival, the wind gets stronger and the waves get bigger.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie held on to the sides of the boat.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack fears a storm is coming.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears thunder far away and sees lightning. He worries that a storm is coming and that it may be part of the danger to the Grand Lady.

paragraphs.context: “Sure,” said Jack. He tried to shake off his worries
paragraphs.simple: Jack tries to stop worrying as the wind and the tide push the boat toward the candles of Carnival.

paragraphs.context: The gondola glided toward a landing at the edge of the canal.
paragraphs.simple: The boat comes to a landing. Water is splashing from the canal onto a wide path full of people at Carnival.

paragraphs.context: The gondolier reached a gloved hand toward Annie
paragraphs.mainIdea: The gondolier has a small hand.
paragraphs.simple: The gondolier helps them out. Jack is surprised that the gondolier's hand feels small, like a child's hand.

paragraphs.context: As soon as Jack had stepped out of the boat
paragraphs.simple: When Jack is out, the gondolier unties the rope, pushes away from the landing and rows off.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie watched the gondola disappear over the choppy waters.
paragraphs.simple: The gondola disappears over the rough water. On the shore, crowds of people in costumes walk up and down the wide path by the canal.

paragraphs.context: Jack saw lots of black cloaks, bird masks, funny hats, and ruffled collars.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees many costumes: chickens, pirates and knights. Nobody cares that water is coming over the edge of the canal and making their shoes wet.

paragraphs.context: As Jack and Annie stared at the crowd, a distant bell began to ring.
paragraphs.simple: A bell far away rings nine times. Jack thinks it is nine o'clock.

paragraphs.context: Just then another bell began to chime.
paragraphs.simple: Then another bell rings ten times. Jack is confused: is it nine or ten o'clock?

paragraphs.context: Annie pointed to a tall woman at the edge of the parade.
paragraphs.simple: Annie points to a tall "woman" with a black mask, lots of jewelry, a white wig and a very wide skirt.

paragraphs.context: “We're looking for someone called the Grand Lady of—”
paragraphs.mainIdea: A giant chicken pulls the man away.
paragraphs.simple: Annie starts to ask, but a person dressed as a giant chicken takes the man's hand and pulls him into the crowd.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, brother,” said Jack, looking around.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Many people are dressed as grand ladies.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees that lots of people are dressed as grand ladies. How can they know which one to visit?

paragraphs.context: “Then let's just skip visiting the Grand Lady of the Lagoon for now,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to go to the next step.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they should not visit the Grand Lady now and asks what Merlin tells them to do next.

paragraphs.context: To find out where you need to go,
paragraphs.simple: To learn where you must go,

paragraphs.context: Seek out a painter named Tiepolo.
paragraphs.simple: look for a painter called Tiepolo.

background.note: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo (1696-1770) was a great painter from Venice. He painted huge, bright pictures on walls and ceilings.

paragraphs.context: As the noisy crowd celebrated around them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack finds Tiepolo in the book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack stands near a lantern and looks in the index of the book. He finds Tiepolo.

paragraphs.context: Tiepolo (say tee-EP-uh-lo) was one of the greatest painters
paragraphs.simple: Tiepolo was one of the greatest painters of Venice in the 1700s. He painted bright, beautiful oil paintings for palaces and big country houses.

paragraphs.context: “If the guy's so famous, people must know where he lives,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks people must know where such a famous man lives. She asks a clown.

paragraphs.context: “But you won't find him home now,” the clown called over his shoulder.
paragraphs.simple: As he walks away, the clown says Tiepolo is not at home. He is painting in Milan.

background.note: Milan is a big city in the north of Italy, about 250 kilometers west of Venice.

paragraphs.context: “Over a day's ride on horseback,” said the clown.
paragraphs.simple: The clown says Milan is more than a day away by horse. Then he disappears into the crowd.

paragraphs.context: “We don't have time,” said Jack. “I think we have to skip Tiepolo, too.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says there is no time to go to Milan, so they must not visit Tiepolo either.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah,” said Annie. “Hey, maybe we should just skip all this stuff
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to find the Ruler of the Seas.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to forget the other steps and find the Ruler of the Seas themselves, because the letter says only he can help save the Grand Lady.

paragraphs.context: “I don't know …,” said Jack. “In his letter, Merlin tells us to be patient—”
paragraphs.simple: Jack is not sure. He reminds Annie that Merlin tells them to be patient.

paragraphs.context: “In the palace on Saint Mark's Square!” said the pirate.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ruler lives in a palace.
paragraphs.simple: A pirate says the ruler lives in the palace on Saint Mark's Square.

background.note: Saint Mark's Square (Piazza San Marco) is the biggest and most famous square in Venice.

paragraphs.context: “I'll look up Saint Mark's Square,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack turns the pages of the book until he finds a map of Venice. He is happy, because he loves maps.

paragraphs.context: “Okay, let's see,” Jack said. “We're here.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack shows where they are on the map and where Saint Mark's Square is. It is very close.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up from the map. Annie was already walking with the crowd.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They arrive at a huge square.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is already walking with the crowd. Jack closes the book and hurries after her. Soon they come to a huge, open square.

paragraphs.context: “Wow,” Jack said breathlessly. Saint Mark's Square was filled with candlelight and musicians.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The square is full of shows.
paragraphs.simple: The square is full of candlelight and music. Acrobats walk on ropes, boxers fight, knights fight with swords, and clowns walk on stilts, race wheelbarrows and try to catch live eels in their mouths.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah,” said Jack. He looked back at their book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack finds a picture of the square in the book and reads about the buildings.

paragraphs.context: The watchtower of Saint Mark's Square is the tallest building in Venice.
paragraphs.simple: The watchtower is the tallest building in Venice. Long ago, the weather vane on top showed sailors where the wind was coming from.

background.note: The bell tower of Saint Mark's (the Campanile) is about 99 meters tall. It fell down in 1902 and was built again.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up. “I can barely see the weather vane up there,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wind is from the south.
paragraphs.simple: Jack can only just see the weather vane. It points north, so he thinks the wind is blowing from the south.

paragraphs.context: The clock tower is one of the most beautiful towers in the world.
paragraphs.simple: The clock tower is very beautiful. On top, a bell is hit every hour by ... (Annie stops him before he finishes.)

background.note: The Clock Tower (Torre dell'Orologio) was built in the 1490s. Two bronze men on top hit the bell every hour.

paragraphs.context: “Jack, skip to the ruler's palace!” interrupted Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to hear about the palace.
paragraphs.simple: Annie stops Jack and asks him to go straight to the part about the ruler's palace.

paragraphs.context: The palace of Venice's ruler is one of the most splendid structures
paragraphs.simple: The ruler's palace is one of the most beautiful buildings ever made. Up to 2,000 important people once met in its great hall. It also has the city's terrible prison rooms. Over the door is a statue of Saint Mark showing a book to a lion with wings.

background.note: This is the Doge's Palace (Palazzo Ducale). The "doge" was the ruler of Venice for about 1,000 years.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up from the map. Annie was heading toward a huge door
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie goes to the palace door.
paragraphs.simple: Annie walks toward a huge door with the statue of a man and a winged lion above it. Jack hurries after her.

paragraphs.context: A guard was standing by the palace door.
paragraphs.simple: A guard in a uniform with a gun stands at the door. Jack wonders if he is a real guard or just someone in a costume.

paragraphs.context: “I'll find out,” said Annie. She walked over to the guard.
paragraphs.simple: Annie politely asks the guard if the ruler of Venice is inside.

paragraphs.context: “I said begone!” the guard growled.
paragraphs.simple: The guard angrily tells them to go away. He is tired of clowns wasting his time.

paragraphs.context: “Go! Both of you! Or else!” roared the guard.
paragraphs.simple: The guard shouts and lifts his gun. Jack is now sure he is a real guard, not someone in a costume.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe it's time to use one of Teddy and Kathleen's rhymes,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks they could turn into ducks to get past the guard.

paragraphs.context: Two clowns on stilts were dancing around the guard.
paragraphs.simple: Two clowns on stilts dance around the guard. One takes his gun and throws it to the other.

paragraphs.context: “Now's our chance!” said Annie. “Quick!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees that this is their chance. She runs to the door and goes in quickly and quietly.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, no—oh, man!” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: While the guard runs after the clowns, Jack hurries to the door and goes in too.

paragraphs.context: Jack found Annie standing behind a column
paragraphs.simple: Jack finds Annie behind a stone post in a courtyard lit by lanterns. It is quiet and empty. Jack thinks everyone is at Carnival and hopes the ruler is home.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked at his map of the palace.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The way to the ruler's rooms.
paragraphs.simple: On the map, some rooms are called the Ruler's Living Chambers. To get there, they must go up the Giants' Stairs.

paragraphs.context: These stairs are called the Giants' Stairs
paragraphs.simple: The stairs have two big statues of Roman gods: Mars, the god of war, and Neptune, the god of the sea.

background.note: Mars was the Roman god of war. The planet Mars is named after him.
Neptune was the Roman god of the sea. He carries a trident (a spear with three points). In Greek stories he is called Poseidon.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie hurried down the passageway
paragraphs.simple: They hurry along a long hall until they reach wide stairs with giant marble statues of strong men on both sides.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie quickly climbed the Giants' Stairs.
paragraphs.simple: They climb the stairs. At the top, Jack says they must turn right and go to the Golden Staircase.

background.note: The Golden Staircase (Scala d'Oro) in the Doge's Palace has a ceiling covered with gold decoration.

paragraphs.context: Keeping an eye out for more guards
paragraphs.mainIdea: They creep to the Golden Staircase.
paragraphs.simple: Watching carefully for guards, they move quietly down a hall to beautiful stairs under a gold ceiling.

paragraphs.context: “There it is,” said Jack. “Let's climb up.”
paragraphs.simple: At the top of the stairs they stop moving. Another guard is leaning against the wall with his eyes closed, snoring quietly.

paragraphs.context: Jack motioned to Annie, and they tiptoed past the sleeping guard
paragraphs.simple: Jack makes a sign to Annie. They walk on their toes past the sleeping guard to the door of the ruler's rooms.

paragraphs.context: The door was open. Jack and Annie peeked inside.
paragraphs.simple: The door is open. They look in, and Annie says "Knock, knock?" quietly. No one answers.

paragraphs.context: They stepped through the doorway. A fire blazed on the hearth.
paragraphs.simple: A big fire burns in the fireplace and many candles burn above. The moving flames make shadows on the marble floor and the carved gold ceiling.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked at their book. “Wait, the next room is the Map Room,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to see the Map Room.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees that the next room is the Map Room and wants to have a quick look.

paragraphs.context: Jack led the way into the Map Room.
paragraphs.simple: Colorful maps hang on the walls, and there are two huge globes. Jack loves this room.

background.note: The Map Room (Sala dello Scudo) in the Doge's Palace has huge painted maps of the world on its walls and two big globes.

paragraphs.context: “Look, more lions,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why are there lions with wings?
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees three paintings of lions with wings and asks why they are everywhere.

paragraphs.context: The winged lion is the symbol of Venice.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The winged lion stands for Venice.
paragraphs.simple: The winged lion is the sign of Venice. It is in paintings and statues all over the city. It means strength on land and at sea.

background.note: The winged lion is the symbol of Saint Mark, the patron saint of Venice. It is on the flag of Venice.

paragraphs.context: As Jack and Annie looked back up at the lion paintings, they heard footsteps.
paragraphs.simple: They hear footsteps. The angry guard and the sleepy guard run into the room.

paragraphs.context: “There they are! The thieves!” the sleepy guard shouted
paragraphs.mainIdea: The guards think they are thieves.
paragraphs.simple: The sleepy guard shouts that they are thieves. He says he heard voices.

paragraphs.context: “We're not thieves,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they are not thieves. They only wanted to find the ruler and ask for help.

paragraphs.context: “Won't admit your crime, eh?” said the grouchy guard.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The guard will put them in a cell.
paragraphs.simple: The angry guard says they will not admit what they did. He says the worst prison rooms are kept for criminals like them.

paragraphs.context: Jack knew there was no use arguing.
paragraphs.simple: Jack knows that arguing will not help. He takes Annie's hand and leaves. The guards walk behind them, pointing guns at their backs.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie walked quickly down the hall, then down some steep, narrow steps.
paragraphs.simple: They go down narrow steps and through a low stone hall, with the guards close behind.

paragraphs.context: “Over the Bridge of Sighs!” shouted the grouchy guard.
paragraphs.simple: The guard tells them to cross the Bridge of Sighs, and to sigh when they cross, because they will not come back for a long time.

background.note: The Bridge of Sighs is a covered stone bridge from the Doge's Palace to the prison. People say prisoners sighed when they saw Venice through its windows for the last time.

paragraphs.context: Jack gripped Annie's hand as they crossed a covered footbridge
paragraphs.simple: Holding Annie's hand tightly, Jack crosses the covered bridge to another building. They walk down a hallway full of water. Jack's shoes are soft and wet.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie stopped in front of a heavy wooden door.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are locked in a cell.
paragraphs.simple: The guard opens a heavy wooden door and pushes them into a dark, wet prison room.

paragraphs.context: The door slammed shut. Jack heard a heavy metal bolt clank into place.
paragraphs.simple: The door shuts loudly. A heavy metal bar locks it. The guards walk away through the water, arguing.

paragraphs.context: The prison was eerily quiet.
paragraphs.simple: The prison is strangely quiet. The air is old and bad, and it is hard to breathe and to see. Only a little light comes through the window with bars. There is a wooden bench under the window.

paragraphs.context: For a moment, Jack couldn't answer. He was stunned.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is too shocked to speak. A few minutes ago they were at the bright Carnival. Now they are locked in a dirty, dark prison.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt shaky as he opened their research book.
paragraphs.simple: Shaking, Jack opens the book by the window, looks up "prison" and reads.

paragraphs.context: The prison cells at ground level in the palace were called the pozzi
paragraphs.simple: The prison rooms on the ground floor were called the "pozzi" (wells or holes). They were wet, had no fresh air, and were full of rats. In the end, even the government thought they were too cruel.

background.note: "Pozzi" is Italian for "wells". These dark, wet cells were on the lowest floor of the Doge's Palace.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard a squeak from a dark corner.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears a squeak in a dark corner. He is very afraid. He wonders if it is a rat.
hardWords: The hair went up on his neck

paragraphs.context: The squeak came again from the dark corner.
paragraphs.simple: More squeaks come from other corners. Jack hears things moving along the walls.

paragraphs.context: “Yep,” said Jack, “definitely.” He kept his eye on the dark corners
paragraphs.mainIdea: They take out the rhyme book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack agrees that they need magic now. He watches the dark corners carefully ("kept his eye on" = watched carefully) while Annie takes out the rhyme book.

paragraphs.context: Annie read from the table of contents:
paragraphs.simple: Annie reads three rhyme names and asks if rats are afraid of ducks.

paragraphs.context: “Forget ducks!” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants the rhyme that makes metal soft. Annie will read it, and he will pull the window bars apart.

paragraphs.context: Jack reached up and felt the iron bars.
paragraphs.simple: The iron bars are cold, hard and strong. Jack cannot imagine bending them.

paragraphs.context: The squeaks were getting louder.
paragraphs.simple: The squeaks get louder. Jack holds two bars, breathes deeply and tells Annie to read.

paragraphs.context: Iron or copper, brass or steel,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The rhyme to make metal soft (line 1).
paragraphs.simple: Iron, copper, brass or steel (different metals),

paragraphs.context: Bree-on-saw! Bro-on-beel!
paragraphs.simple: These are magic words in Teddy's and Kathleen's languages. They have no meaning in English.

paragraphs.context: As Annie finished the rhyme, the bars began to glow.
paragraphs.simple: The bars start to shine and get warm in Jack's hands.

paragraphs.context: Holding the bars tightly Jack pulled in opposite directions.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pulls the bars away from each other. Slowly they get longer and bend, until there is a hole big enough for them to go through.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard a chorus of squeaks from all sides of the cell.
paragraphs.simple: Many squeaks come from all around. Jack sees the dark shapes of many rats smelling the air under the window.

paragraphs.context: Annie squeezed between the bars and jumped down into the hallway.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pushes through the bars and jumps down into the hallway. Jack follows, lands on the wet floor and gets up quickly.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie sloshed down the watery hallway.
paragraphs.simple: They splash down the wet hallway and almost run into the two guards. They keep running.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie dodged away from them.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie move quickly to the side. The guards run into each other and fall. Jack and Annie run across the Bridge of Sighs and up the stone steps.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie bounded down the Golden Staircase two steps at a time.
paragraphs.simple: They jump down the stairs two at a time, run very fast past the statues of Mars and Neptune and out of the palace into Saint Mark's Square.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie ran through the square, dodging dancers
paragraphs.simple: They run across the square, moving quickly around dancers, fortune-tellers and acrobats. They stop in the middle of a crowd watching a puppet show, where no one can see them.

paragraphs.context: As Jack tried to catch his breath
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathes hard. He sees many people in pirate, animal and clown costumes, so he is glad their silly clothes help them hide. They laugh, but they are still nervous.

paragraphs.context: “We should have been more patient.
paragraphs.simple: Annie agrees that they should have waited. She wants to go back to the part about the painter Tiepolo.

paragraphs.context: Jack nodded. “I think we should go to his house,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to go to Tiepolo's house. Maybe the painter is at home, and the clown was wrong when he said Tiepolo was away.

paragraphs.context: “The clown said Tiepolo lives near the Church of San Felice,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack looks carefully at the map and follows the way from Saint Mark's Square to the church with his finger. He tells Annie to stay in the dark places, because the guards may be looking for them.

background.note: San Felice is a small, old church in the north part of Venice, not far from the Grand Canal.

paragraphs.context: Jack stuffed the book into his backpack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pushes the book into his backpack. Holding hands, they push through the crowd to a narrow street.

paragraphs.context: The wind was blowing harder as Jack and Annie headed

paragraphs.context: She pointed at a gondola docked nearby.

paragraphs.context: “Great!” said Annie. “Bye, Lorenzo! Thanks!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says goodbye to Lorenzo, and they hurry to the landing where the gondola is waiting.

paragraphs.context: The gondolier silently helped Jack and Annie into the boat.
paragraphs.simple: Without a word, the gondolier helps them into the boat. He unties it and pushes away from the landing.

paragraphs.context: As the boat glided through the shallow waters, Jack looked back at Venice.

paragraphs.context: The gondola moved around the bend and up the narrow canal near the walled garden.

background.note: In Venice, boats are tied to tall wooden poles in the water. Many are painted with stripes.

paragraphs.context: As the gondolier helped Jack onto the landing, the boat rocked in the water.
paragraphs.simple: The boat moves, Jack trips and pulls the glove off the gondolier's hand.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, sorry,” said Jack. As he handed the glove back, he gasped.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees a pale blue glass ring on the gondolier's finger, like Teddy and Kathleen's magic rings.

paragraphs.context: Before Jack could say anything, the gondolier pulled his glove back on
paragraphs.simple: The gondolier quickly puts the glove back on and pushes the boat away.

paragraphs.context: “Hey—hey!” Jack sputtered.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack calls to Teddy and Kathleen.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is so surprised that he can hardly speak. He calls Teddy and Kathleen to come back.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie watched the gondola disappear into a blaze of sunlight
paragraphs.simple: The gondola goes into the bright sunlight on the water. Did it go around the corner, or did it disappear by magic?

paragraphs.context: “Well, I guess anybody could wear a glass ring,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says anyone could wear a glass ring. But he still thinks it was them.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe Morgan and Merlin told them to watch over us,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy and Kathleen kept them safe.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks Morgan and Merlin may have asked Teddy and Kathleen to look after them.

paragraphs.context: “Right,” said Jack. “Well, Venice wasn't destroyed by a flood.
paragraphs.simple: Venice was not destroyed, so Jack thinks they passed their first test.

paragraphs.context: With Lorenzo's canvas tucked under his arm
paragraphs.simple: Jack carries Lorenzo's canvas under his arm and goes into the garden to the rope ladder.

paragraphs.context: When they climbed into the tree house, Jack pulled Merlin's letter
paragraphs.simple: In the tree house, Jack points to the words "Frog Creek" on Merlin's letter and wishes to go home.

paragraphs.context: Then everything was still.
paragraphs.simple: Then everything stops moving. It is completely quiet.

paragraphs.context: A nippy wind rustled the Frog Creek trees.
paragraphs.simple: A cold wind moves the trees. They are wearing their own clothes again. It is early morning.

paragraphs.context: “I'm glad Lorenzo gave us his painting to finish,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Lorenzo gave them his painting to finish. Jack says it will be like having their trip again.

paragraphs.context: “Wait,” said Annie. “Don't you think we should take the book of rhymes with us?

paragraphs.simple: Jack says they cannot use the rhymes at home, but they will keep the book safe until the next mission.

paragraphs.context: As they walked through the chilly dawn woods, Annie held up Lorenzo's canvas.
paragraphs.simple: Annie holds up the canvas. The shining light and water of Venice look just like real life. She asks what they should paint in it.

paragraphs.context: “And the old man and Rosa walking along the canal,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to paint the old man and his dog Rosa walking by the canal, and of course Lorenzo.

paragraphs.context: “With Neptune himself peeking out!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to show just the top of Neptune's head and his strange eyes.

paragraphs.context: “We'll paint ourselves on the back of the lion,” said Jack,
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they will paint themselves on the lion's back in their clown clothes and red slippers.

paragraphs.context: A chilly dawn breeze swept through the bare trees.
paragraphs.simple: A cold morning wind blows through the trees. A church bell rings, and Jack and Annie start running home.

paragraphs.context: Venice has been called a “timeless city,”
paragraphs.simple: People call Venice a "timeless city", because much of the city and its old ways have been kept the same for a very long time.

paragraphs.context: The festival of Carnival goes back over a thousand years in Venice
paragraphs.simple: Carnival in Venice is more than 1,000 years old, but it was most popular in the 1700s.

paragraphs.context: Gondolas have glided along the waterways of Venice for over a thousand years.
paragraphs.simple: Gondolas have been used for more than 1,000 years. In the 1700s there were about 14,000; today there are about 400.

paragraphs.context: Saint Mark the Apostle is the patron saint of Venice.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Saint Mark and the winged lion.
paragraphs.simple: Saint Mark is the special saint of Venice. A story says his body was taken from its grave and brought to Venice in the 800s. His sign is a winged lion, so winged lions are everywhere in the city: at least fourteen in Saint Mark's Square alone.

background.note: Saint Mark wrote one of the four Gospels (books about the life of Jesus) in the Bible. In 828, merchants from Venice took his body from Alexandria in Egypt.

paragraphs.context: In Venice, there are approximately 3,000 alleys and 200 canals.
paragraphs.simple: Venice has about 3,000 narrow streets and 200 canals. More than 400 bridges join its 118 islands.

paragraphs.context: Many world-famous painters are from Venice.
paragraphs.simple: Many famous painters come from Venice. Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was the most important in the 1700s. His sons Giandomenico and Lorenzo were painters too.

paragraphs.context: Neptune is the Roman counterpart of the sea god Poseidon
paragraphs.simple: Neptune is the Roman version of the Greek sea god Poseidon. His spear with three points is called a trident. The planet Neptune has a trident as its sign.

background.note: Neptune is the eighth and farthest planet from the sun. It was discovered in 1846. Its symbol looks like a trident.

paragraphs.context: Whenever I start work on a new Magic Tree House book
paragraphs.simple: For each book, the writer does research: she goes to libraries, uses the Internet, visits bookshops and museums, talks to people who know a lot, and visits the place if she can.

paragraphs.context: I chose to write a Magic Tree House story about Venice
paragraphs.simple: The writer wanted to visit Venice again. She remembered a warm summer night in Saint Mark's Square, with beautiful buildings, candles on café tables and violin music. Writing a book gave her a good reason to go back.

background.note: "Piazza San Marco" is Italian for "Saint Mark's Square". "Piazza" means square.

paragraphs.context: On my second trip to Venice, I brought my guide book, camera, and notebook.
paragraphs.simple: On her second trip, she visited museums, bought books of Carnival costume paintings, took photos of the towers and took notes in the Doge's Palace, including Tiepolo's painting of Neptune and Venice.

background.note: The "doge" was the elected ruler of Venice from about 700 to 1797. The Doge's Palace was his home and the center of the government.

paragraphs.context: My most unforgettable experience in the Doge's Palace
paragraphs.mainIdea: A visit to the old prison.
paragraphs.simple: The writer will never forget the old prison in the palace. She walked through narrow, wet halls and over the Bridge of Sighs to the empty cells, and drew the windows and doors in her notebook.

paragraphs.context: As I tried to leave, I became confused about how to get out of the prison.
paragraphs.mainIdea: She got lost in the prison.
paragraphs.simple: She could not find the way out of the prison. Out of breath, with her heart beating fast, she hurried through the old-smelling halls and up and down the stairs.

paragraphs.context: Finally I found my way back out onto the beautiful, sunny square.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Now she knew how Jack and Annie feel.
paragraphs.simple: At last she got out into the sunny square. She thought that now she really knew how Jack and Annie would feel in the prison.

paragraphs.context: On the morning I left Venice, I rode in a gondola
paragraphs.simple: On her last morning she rode in a gondola, took notes and photographs, and tried to record the beauty of the city. But no photo or note can really show how wonderful Venice is. It lives best in your memory and imagination.

sentences.grammar: "Be about to" means be going to do something very soon. "Just as" means at the same moment.

sentences.context: It was damp from the floodwaters, but all the writing was as clear as ever.
sentences.simple: It was a little wet from the flood, but all the writing was still as clear as before.

parts.text: It was damp from the floodwaters,
parts.meaning: It was a little wet from the flood,

parts.text: but all the writing was as clear as ever.
parts.meaning: but all the writing was still clear.

sentences.grammar: "But" joins two different ideas. "As clear as ever" means as clear as it always was.

sentences.context: Had it just glided around the bend? Or had it vanished altogether?
sentences.simple: Did it just go around the corner? Or did it disappear completely by magic?

parts.text: Had it just glided around the bend?
parts.meaning: Did it only go around the corner?

parts.text: Or had it vanished altogether?
parts.meaning: Or did it disappear completely?

sentences.grammar: Questions in the past perfect: "Had it ...?" Jack asks about something that happened just before. "Altogether" means completely.

sentences.context: But no photographs can truly do Venice justice.
sentences.simple: But no photos can really show how wonderful Venice is.
sentences.main: No photographs can do Venice justice.

parts.text: But no photographs
parts.meaning: But no photos

parts.meaning: can really show how good Venice is.

sentences.grammar: "Do someone/something justice" is an idiom: show how good it really is. "No + noun" means not any.

a couple of.example: “They just think we're a couple of ragged clowns.”
a couple of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

about to.meaning: Going to happen or do something very soon.
about to.example: as if a storm was about to break.
about to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

according to.meaning: As said or shown by someone or something.
according to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

after all.meaning: In spite of what people thought or said before. "Maybe he's there after all" means maybe he is there, though the clown said he was away.
after all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

all over again.example: That'll be like living our trip all over again.
all over again.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

as well.example: it seems our magic sent us to dreamland as well.
as well.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

as well as.example: as well as a city “frozen in time.”
as well as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

back and forth.meaning: First one way, then the other way, again and again.
back and forth.example: His tufted tail swayed back and forth.
back and forth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

be dying to.meaning: To want to do something very much.
be dying to.example: I was dying to go back to Venice.
be dying to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

be supposed to.meaning: 1. Should; to be expected to do something ("What are we supposed to do first?"). 2. "Is supposed to be" can also mean is meant to show ("the lady in the painting is supposed to be the city of Venice").
be supposed to.example: “What are we supposed to do first?”
be supposed to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

broke in.meaning: Started talking while another person was talking; interrupted. ("Broke in" is the past of "break in".)
broke in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

bump into.meaning: To hit against someone or something by accident.
bump into.example: they nearly bumped right into the two guards.
bump into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

call for.meaning: To ask someone to come to you.
call for.example: he will call for you again soon.
call for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

calm down.meaning: To become calm, not excited or worried.
calm down.example: “Calm down. We just have to be patient,”
calm down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

can't help.meaning: "Can't help doing something" means you cannot stop yourself from doing it. "He couldn't help worrying" means he could not stop worrying.
can't help.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

catch up with.meaning: To reach someone who is ahead of you by going faster.
catch up with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch your breath.meaning: 1. To stop breathing for a moment because you are surprised ("Jack caught his breath"). 2. To rest until you can breathe normally again, after running ("Jack tried to catch his breath").
catch your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

clean up.meaning: To make a place clean by taking away dirt and trash.
clean up.example: two sweepers were cleaning up the remains of Carnival.
clean up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

clear your throat.meaning: To cough a little before you speak, so your voice is clear or to get attention.
clear your throat.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

clock tower.meaning: A tall tower with a big clock on it.
clock tower.example: The clock tower is one of the most beautiful towers in the world.
clock tower.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

come alive.meaning: To start living; (of a statue) to become a living thing.
come alive.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come into your mind.example: The details of Tiepolo's painting came into his mind.
come into your mind.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come to a stop.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come true.meaning: (Of a dream or wish) to really happen.
come true.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

dead end.meaning: A point where you cannot go on and must stop or try another way. (Also: a street that is closed at one end.)
dead end.example: They'd come to another dead end.
dead end.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

do justice.meaning: To "do something justice" means to show how good or beautiful it really is.
do justice.example: no photographs can truly do Venice justice.
do justice.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

draw near.example: As they drew near the golden angel
draw near.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

fast asleep.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: To find out where you need to go,
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

fit through.meaning: To be small enough to go through an opening.
fit through.example: large enough for Annie and him to fit through.
fit through.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

from memory.meaning: Without looking at the words, because you have learned them.
from memory.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get along to.meaning: To go to a place, now. "Get along to the fireworks" means go to the fireworks now.
get along to.example: But you should get along to the fireworks on the waterfront now.
get along to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

give someone a ride.meaning: To take someone somewhere in your car or your boat.
give someone a ride.example: “Can you give us a ride back to the island?”
give someone a ride.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

give way to.meaning: To be followed by something and replaced by it.
give way to.example: The red showers gave way to bursts of blue and green.
give way to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

give yourself over to.meaning: To stop trying to control something and let it carry you or take you along.
give yourself over to.example: as he gave himself over to the lion's wondrous powers of flight.
give yourself over to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

go on.meaning: 1. To go on a trip or a mission ("Where are we going on our first mission?"). 2. "What's going on?" means what is happening? 3. To go on with something; to continue ("went on her way" = walked on).
go on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

go out.meaning: (Of a fire or a light) to stop burning.
go out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

goose bumps.meaning: Small raised spots on your skin that come when you are cold, scared or very excited.
goose bumps.example: He felt goose bumps on his skin.
goose bumps.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

got it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

guess what.meaning: "Guess what!" You say this just before you tell someone surprising news.
guess what.example: “Hey, guess what! We saw Neptune last night,”
guess what.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

had better.meaning: Should. "We'd better hurry" means we should hurry.
had better.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hang on.meaning: 1. To hold on tightly ("Hang on!" = hold on tight!). 2. "Maps hung on the walls" means the maps were hanging on the walls.
hang on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

have no idea.example: and we have no idea who she is.
have no idea.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

have something to do with.example: it must have something to do with water,
have something to do with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold on.meaning: To hold something tightly so that you do not fall. "Hold on to" means hold something tightly.
hold on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hold up.meaning: To lift something and hold it high, so people can see it.
hold up.example: He held up his candle to show a painting
hold up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in an instant.example: In an instant, his shaggy mane, golden back, powerful legs, tufted tail, and feathered wings all turned to carved gray stone.
in an instant.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in case.meaning: Because something might happen. "Stay in the shadows in case the guards come" means stay hidden, because the guards might come.
in case.example: Stay in the shadows in case those guards come looking for us.
in case.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in fact.meaning: Really; the truth is. People say "in fact" to add something more surprising.
in fact.example: In fact, I think I see a light now inside Tiepolo's house.
in fact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in the background.meaning: At the back of a picture, behind the main things.
in the background.example: we could paint the clock tower in the background
in the background.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the distance.example: In the distance, thousands of candles twinkled along the shoreline.
in the distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

into place.example: a heavy metal bolt clank into place.
into place.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep an eye out for.meaning: To watch carefully for someone or something.
keep an eye out for.example: Keeping an eye out for more guards
keep an eye out for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

lead the way.meaning: To go first, to show other people where to go.
lead the way.example: Jack led the way into the Map Room.
lead the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let out.meaning: To make a sound, like a cry or a roar.
let out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

let someone know.example: send dreams to let you know we were here
let someone know.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

lock up.meaning: To lock all the doors of a building, for example when you close a shop for the night.
lock up.example: a young woman locking up a café.
lock up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look up.meaning: 1. To raise your eyes and look up ("Jack looked up from the map"). 2. To look for a word or a fact in a book ("Jack looked up carnival in the index").
look up.example: Jack looked up from the map. Annie was already walking
look up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

make sense.meaning: To be easy to understand; to seem right. "That makes no sense" means I cannot understand it.
make sense.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

make sure.meaning: To check, or to do something, so that you are sure about something.
make sure.example: to make sure we'd be safe
make sure.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

much less.meaning: And certainly not. "Not even one man, much less two" means not even one man, so of course not two.
much less.example: not even one man, much less two.
much less.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no fewer than.meaning: As many as (said when a number is surprisingly big).
no fewer than.example: there are no fewer than fourteen!
no fewer than.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no kidding.meaning: "Really! That is true!" You say it to agree strongly with something that is clear.
no kidding.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no longer.meaning: Not now, though it was before.
no longer.example: The weather vane was no longer pointing north with the winds.
no longer.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

oh, boy.meaning: What you say when you are excited or happy (sometimes when you are worried). It is not about a boy.

oh, brother.meaning: What you say when you feel a little tired of something or a little annoyed. It is not about a real brother.

oh, man.meaning: What you say when you feel strongly: surprised, afraid, tired or happy. It is like "Oh, wow!" or "Oh, no!" It is not about a man.

on your own.meaning: Alone, without help from other people.
on your own.example: “Morgan thinks you may be ready to use magic on your own,”
on your own.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

one thing at a time.meaning: "One thing (or one step) at a time" means do things slowly, one after another, not all together.
one thing at a time.example: “Let's just take one thing at a time,”
one thing at a time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

or else.meaning: "Or else!" means "If you don't do it, something bad will happen to you!" It is a warning.
or else.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

over your shoulder.meaning: Behind you, turning your head back. "Called over his shoulder" means said something while walking away, turning his head back a little.
over your shoulder.example: the clown called over his shoulder.
over your shoulder.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pay attention.meaning: To watch, listen or think carefully about something.
pay attention.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pick at.meaning: (Of a bird) to take small bits of food with its beak, again and again.
pick at.example: picking at orange peels, squashed grapes, torn ribbons, and feathers.
pick at.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pick up.meaning: 1. To lift something up or take it in your hand ("Jack picked up his backpack"). 2. (Of wind) to become stronger ("the wind picked up").
pick up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

prove yourself.meaning: To show other people that you are good, brave or able to do something.
prove yourself.example: Morgan has convinced Merlin to let you prove yourselves.
prove yourself.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pull apart.meaning: To pull two things away from each other.
pull apart.example: I'll try to pull the bars apart.
pull apart.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pull away.meaning: 1. To move away from someone or something ("he pulled away from the two of them"). 2. To pull someone so that they go away with you ("pulled him away into the crowd").
pull away.example: Then he pulled away from the two of them
pull away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pull off.meaning: To take something off by pulling it.
pull off.example: He pulled off the cloth cover.
pull off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

push off.meaning: To push a boat away from the land with an oar or your hand, to start moving.
push off.example: pushed off from the landing, and began rowing away.
push off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

push your way.meaning: To move through a crowd by pushing people.
push your way.example: Jack and Annie pushed their way back through the crowd.
push your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

put away.meaning: To put something back in its usual place.
put away.example: Jack closed the book and put it away.
put away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

put out.meaning: To put things outside or on a table so people can see them. "Putting out goods to sell" means putting things out so people can buy them.
put out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

roller coaster.meaning: A ride at a fun fair: small cars on a track that go up and down and around very fast.
roller coaster.example: “I hope it has a roller coaster.”
roller coaster.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

scramble to your feet.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

seek out.meaning: To look for someone or something until you find them.
seek out.example: Seek out a painter named Tiepolo.
seek out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

shake off.meaning: To get rid of a bad feeling.
shake off.example: He tried to shake off his worries
shake off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

slip off.meaning: To take off clothes or a bag quickly and easily.
slip off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stand for.meaning: To be a sign of something; to mean something.
stand for.example: the lions stand for strength on both land and sea.
stand for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

table of contents.meaning: The list of chapters or parts at the front of a book, with their page numbers.
table of contents.example: Annie opened the book to the table of contents.
table of contents.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm before something hard.
take a deep breath.example: Jack took a deep breath and stroked the lion's golden mane.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take a look.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take notes.meaning: To write down short facts, so that you can remember them.
take notes.example: took notes on the statues of Neptune and Mars
take notes.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take off.meaning: "Take off running" means suddenly start running.
take off.example: Jack and Annie took off running for home.
take off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the hair went up on his neck.meaning: He suddenly felt very afraid (people say the hair on your neck stands up when you are scared).
the hair went up on his neck.example: The hair went up on his neck.
the hair went up on his neck.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

there is no use.meaning: "There is no use doing something" means doing it will not help.
there is no use.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

throw on.meaning: To put on clothes quickly, without care.
throw on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

tie up.meaning: To tie a boat to something so that it does not float away.
tie up.example: As the gondolier tied up the boat
tie up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn into.meaning: To change and become something different.
turn into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

two steps at a time.meaning: Going up or down stairs by jumping over every other step, to go very fast.
two steps at a time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wake up.meaning: 1. To stop sleeping ("Jack, wake up!"). 2. (Of a town) to become busy in the morning, when people start their day ("Venice starting to wake up").
wake up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

watch over.meaning: To look after someone and keep them safe.
watch over.example: told them to watch over us
watch over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

weather vane.meaning: A metal object on top of a building that turns to show which way the wind is blowing.
weather vane.example: The weather vane on top once helped sailors
weather vane.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

with all your might.meaning: With all your strength; as hard as you can.
with all your might.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.
